usage: 깊다 (deep) is the natural pairing for a close bond
쌓다 (to stack up) = build over time, very common collocation
진정한 (genuine) is the set adjective you'll hear in dramas and toasts
금이 가다 = a crack forms; idiomatic for a damaged relationship
examples: 10년 우정인데 돈 문제로 이렇게 멀어질 줄 몰랐어.
We've been friends for 10 years; I never thought money would push us apart like this.
멀어지다 = grow distant; banmal between close friends
힘들 때 곁에 있어 주는 게 진짜 우정이죠.
Being by your side when times are hard is real friendship.
곁에 있어 주다 = stay by one's side; polite reflective tone
둘이 우정이 정말 끈끈하네요.
The bond between you two is really tight.
끈끈하다 = sticky/tight, a warm compliment about closeness
nuance: 우정 is the abstract concept of friendship (the bond itself), not a friend — the person is 친구. You build it over time with 쌓다 and describe it as deep (깊다) or tight (끈끈하다). It carries a slightly weighty, sincere feeling, so Koreans use it for meaningful long-term bonds rather than casual acquaintances.
mistakes: Using 우정 to mean 'a friend' — the person is 친구; 우정 is the relationship
Saying 우정을 만들다 (make a friendship); the idiomatic verb is 쌓다 (build up) or 나누다 (share)

usage: 신뢰가 가다 = trust comes naturally; the everyday way to say 'I trust them'
쌓다 again — trust is built up over time
잃다 = lose; what happens after a betrayal or broken promise
무너지다 = crumble/collapse, stronger than just 잃다
examples: 한 번 거짓말하면 신뢰가 무너져요.
Lie once and trust collapses.
Common life lesson tone; 무너지다 stresses total breakdown
저 사람은 말한 건 꼭 지켜서 신뢰가 가.
That person always keeps their word, so I trust them.
지키다 = keep (a promise); banmal
회사에서 신뢰를 쌓으려면 시간이 걸려요.
Building trust at work takes time.
Practical workplace reality; -(으)려면 = if you want to
nuance: 신뢰 is trust as a noun, more formal and considered than the verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). You say 신뢰가 가다 ('trust flows') when someone earns your confidence, and 신뢰가 무너지다 when it breaks. It fits relationships, workplaces, and institutions alike — broader and more 'serious' than casual belief.
mistakes: Conjugating it like a verb (신뢰해요 exists, but for the noun use 신뢰가 가다 / 신뢰를 쌓다)
Confusing 신뢰 (earned, reasoned trust) with 믿음 (belief/faith), which can be more emotional or religious

english: loyalty, sense of duty to people
usage: to be loyal / have a sense of duty
의리가 있다 = the standard way to praise someone's loyalty
지키다 = uphold; staying loyal through hard times
to be disloyal / a fair-weather friend
없다 version is a common complaint; drops 가 in casual speech
의리로 = on the basis of loyalty; often + 뭉치다 (band together)
examples: 야, 친구끼리 이러면 의리 없는 거지.
Hey, doing this to a friend is just disloyal.
친구끼리 = between friends; classic banmal guilt-trip
우리 형은 의리 하나는 진짜 끝내줘.
If there's one thing my older brother has, it's loyalty.
끝내주다 = be awesome; 하나는 highlights one standout trait
의리 때문에 끝까지 도와줬어요.
I helped them to the end out of loyalty.
끝까지 = to the very end; -때문에 gives the reason
nuance: 의리 is a deeply Korean value: staying faithful to friends, family, or your crew even when it costs you. It's tied to not abandoning people and repaying what you owe emotionally. You'll hear it constantly among friends ('의리 없냐?') and in films about brotherhood. It's warmer and more personal than formal 충성 (allegiance).
mistakes: Translating it as plain 'loyalty' to a company/country — that's 충성; 의리 is loyalty to people you have a bond with
Forgetting it's often used bare in speech: '의리 없어' rather than always '의리가 없어'

usage: 생기다 = come into being; the default verb for conflict starting
Common compound; also 부부 갈등 (marital), 노사 갈등 (labor-management)
examples: 룸메이트랑 청소 문제로 갈등이 좀 있어요.
I'm having some friction with my roommate over cleaning.
Very real shared-housing scenario; -랑 = with (casual)
갈등이 생기면 바로 대화로 푸는 게 좋아요.
When conflict comes up, it's best to resolve it right away by talking.
대화로 풀다 = resolve through conversation
팀 안에서 갈등이 깊어지고 있어요.
The conflict within the team is deepening.
깊어지다 = grow deeper; workplace context
nuance: 갈등 covers interpersonal friction and inner dilemmas alike, but in daily life it usually means tension or clashing between people. It's more neutral and 'situational' than 싸움 (a fight/quarrel) — you can have 갈등 without ever raising your voice. You 풀다 (untie) it, not 'win' it.
mistakes: Using 갈등 for a loud argument — that moment is 싸움 or 다툼; 갈등 is the underlying tension
Saying 갈등을 이기다 (win the conflict); you 풀다 (resolve) or 해결하다 it, you don't win it

usage: 풀다 = untie; exactly the verb you need to apologize
Verb form; 오해했어요 = I misunderstood / I got it wrong
오해하지 마 = super common reassurance among friends
examples: 아, 그거 오해예요. 그런 뜻 아니었어요.
Ah, that's a misunderstanding. I didn't mean it that way.
그런 뜻 아니었어요 = I didn't mean it like that; defusing tension
오해하지 마, 너 욕한 거 아니야.
Don't get the wrong idea, I wasn't badmouthing you.
Reassuring a friend in banmal; 욕하다 = badmouth/curse
빨리 만나서 오해를 푸는 게 좋겠어요.
We'd better meet soon and clear up the misunderstanding.
-는 게 좋겠어요 = it'd be best to; gentle suggestion
nuance: 오해 is a misunderstanding where someone reads a situation or your intent wrong. The key phrase for fixing it is 오해를 풀다 (untie the misunderstanding). '오해하지 마' is one of the most useful relationship phrases you'll ever learn — it heads off conflict before it grows. Note 오해 (wrong understanding) vs 착각 (a mistaken impression, often about oneself).
mistakes: Saying 오해를 고치다 (fix a misunderstanding); the idiom is 오해를 풀다 (untie it)
Mixing up 오해 (misreading someone/something) with 착각 (a personal delusion or mix-up)

usage: 늘어놓다 = lay out at length; emphasizes nonstop trash-talk
뒤에서 = behind the back; the typical setting
남 = other people; 남 험담 = talking trash about others
examples: 다른 사람 험담하는 거 별로 안 좋아해요.
I don't really like badmouthing other people.
별로 안 좋아하다 = not really a fan of; polite distancing
걔는 맨날 뒤에서 동료 험담만 해.
She does nothing but badmouth coworkers behind their backs.
맨날 = every single day; banmal complaint
험담은 결국 돌고 돌아 본인한테 와요.
Badmouthing eventually goes around and comes back to you.
돌고 돌아 = going around and around; proverb-like warning
nuance: 험담 is speaking ill of someone, with a clearly negative, malicious edge — it's not neutral gossip. It overlaps heavily with 뒷담화 (talking behind someone's back), but 험담 stresses the cruel content of the words, while 뒷담화 stresses the behind-the-back act. Saying you dislike 험담 signals good character.
mistakes: Using 험담 for neutral chit-chat or rumors — that's 소문 or just 수다; 험담 is always negative
Treating 험담 as harmless gossip; it implies real ill will, so it's stronger than English 'gossip'

usage: 까다 = a slangy verb for dishing dirt; very colloquial
to overhear/be the target of back-talk
듣다 here = to catch wind that you were talked about
대상 = object/target; who everyone is talking about
examples: 내 뒷담화 한 거 다 들었거든?
I heard everything you said about me behind my back, okay?
-거든 adds a pointed 'just so you know' tone; banmal
회식에서 상사 뒷담화 까는 건 위험해요.
Trash-talking your boss at a company dinner is risky.
까다 = slangy 'dish on'; 회식 = company dinner
뒷담화하지 말고 그냥 본인한테 말해.
Don't talk behind their back, just tell them directly.
본인한테 = to the person themselves; practical advice in banmal
nuance: 뒷담화 (literally 'back-talk') is the act of gossiping about someone who isn't present. The slangy combo 뒷담화 까다 is what young Koreans actually say among friends. It's a notch more casual than 험담 and focuses on the sneaky behind-the-back nature rather than purely cruel words. Extremely common in office and friend-group talk.
mistakes: Spelling it 뒷담하 or 뒤담화 — it's 뒷담화 (뒤 + ㅅ + 담화)
Using it for praise said behind someone's back; 뒷담화 is by default negative

english: social awareness, ability to read the room
usage: to be quick to read situations
빠르다 = fast; the highest compliment for social skills
없다 = lacking; can't read the room at all
to read someone's mood / walk on eggshells
보다 = watch; checking how others feel before acting
written as one word; 눈치챘어 = I caught on / I noticed
examples: 눈치 좀 챙겨. 지금 그 말 할 때 아니야.
Read the room. Now's not the time to say that.
눈치 챙기다 = get some social sense; sharp banmal
저는 눈치가 없어서 분위기를 잘 못 읽어요.
I'm a bit clueless, so I don't read the mood well.
분위기를 읽다 = read the atmosphere; humble self-description
사장님 눈치 보느라 일찍 못 가요.
I can't leave early because I'm watching the boss's mood.
-느라 = because of (doing); classic office reality
nuance: 눈치 is one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. 눈치가 빠르다 (quick eye) is high praise; 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism. 눈치를 보다 means reading someone's mood, often a superior's. Living in Korea, you'll use and need this word constantly.
mistakes: Translating it as just 'eyes' — 눈치 is the social skill of reading people, not vision
Confusing 눈치를 보다 (read someone's mood, often cautiously) with 눈치를 채다 (notice/catch on)

usage: to have a connection / be fated to meet
있다 = there is; suggests fate brought you together
for a connection to come about
닿다 = to reach/touch; poetic 'fate connected us'
a good connection / good people to know
끊다 = cut off; ending a relationship for good
examples: 이렇게 또 만나다니, 우리 인연인가 봐요.
Meeting again like this — I guess we're fated.
-나 봐요 = I guess/it seems; light, warm tone
여기서 좋은 인연 많이 만들었어요.
I made a lot of good connections here.
Said when leaving a job or city; 만들다 here is idiomatic
그 사람하고는 인연이 아니었나 봐.
I guess that person and I just weren't meant to be.
Used after a breakup or falling-out; reflective banmal
nuance: 인연 is the idea that some meetings are destined — it carries a soft, almost spiritual feeling rooted in Buddhist thought. It applies to romance, friendships, mentors, even chance encounters. '우리 인연인가 봐' is a sweet, slightly flirty line. Ending things is 인연을 끊다. It's warmer and more fateful than the plain 관계 (relationship).
mistakes: Using 인연 as a neutral word for any 'relationship' — that's 관계; 인연 implies fate/destiny
Saying 인연을 만나다 (meet a fate); you say 인연이 있다 / 인연이 닿다 or 인연을 만들다

usage: 당하다 = to suffer/have done to you; the passive everyday form
하다 verb; 배신했어 = you betrayed me
-감 = sense/feeling; 배신감 드는 게 = the betrayed feeling that comes
Literally 'hit the back of the head'; vivid synonym for betraying
examples: 믿었던 친구한테 배신당해서 너무 힘들어.
I'm having a really hard time after being betrayed by a friend I trusted.
믿었던 = whom I had trusted; raw banmal
그렇게 뒤통수를 칠 줄은 몰랐어요.
I never expected them to stab me in the back like that.
뒤통수 치다 = backstab; -ㄹ 줄 몰랐다 = didn't expect
배신감 때문에 한동안 아무도 못 믿었어요.
Because of the sense of betrayal, I couldn't trust anyone for a while.
한동안 = for a while; 배신감 = feeling of betrayal
nuance: 배신 is betrayal — breaking someone's trust or loyalty, a heavy and emotional word. You're usually on the receiving end with 배신을 당하다. The vivid idiom 뒤통수(를) 치다 ('hit the back of the head') is what people often say in casual speech for being backstabbed. 배신감 (the feeling) is just as commonly used as the act itself.
mistakes: Using 배신 for minor letdowns — it's strong, for real broken trust, not mild disappointment (실망)
Forgetting the passive: to say 'I was betrayed' use 배신당하다, not just 배신하다 (which means you did the betraying)

english: yielding, giving way, deferring to others
usage: 자리 = seat; the classic subway/bus courtesy
to compromise / each give a little
서로 = each other; the spirit of meeting halfway
give a little / cut me some slack
Casual plea to be more flexible; banmal
examples: 지하철에서 할머니께 자리를 양보했어요.
I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
-께 = honorific 'to'; a daily act of courtesy in Korea
둘 다 조금씩 양보하면 금방 해결돼요.
If you each give a little, it'll be sorted out quickly.
조금씩 = little by little; advice for resolving conflict
이번엔 내가 양보할게. 네가 골라.
I'll give in this time. You pick.
-ㄹ게 = I'll (do it); friendly banmal
nuance: 양보 is the act of yielding — giving up your seat, your turn, or your preference for someone else's sake. It's a prized social virtue in Korea, especially toward elders (자리를 양보하다 on the subway is everyday courtesy). In disagreements, 서로 양보하다 means meeting halfway. It's voluntary and gracious, not losing or being forced to give in (양보 ≠ 포기).
mistakes: Confusing 양보 (graciously yielding to someone) with 포기 (giving up on a goal entirely)
Using it only for seats — it also covers yielding your turn, opinion, or right-of-way while driving (양보 운전)

usage: 하다 verb; 화해했어요 = we made up
to make up first / extend the olive branch
먼저 = first; being the one to reach out
손길 = a hand/touch; reaching out to make peace
examples: 우리 이제 그만 싸우고 화해하자.
Let's stop fighting now and make up.
-자 = let's; warm banmal between close people
내가 먼저 화해하려고 연락했어요.
I reached out first to make up.
먼저 화해하다 = be the first to reconcile; -려고 = intending to
부부 싸움 후에 금방 화해했어요.
We made up quickly after the couple's spat.
부부 싸움 = marital spat; 금방 = quickly
nuance: 화해 is making peace after a fight or falling-out — restoring a damaged relationship. The verb 화해하다 is what you use with friends, partners, and family ('우리 화해하자'). Being the bigger person and reaching out is 먼저 화해하다, which Koreans see as mature and warm. It pairs naturally with the aftermath of 싸움 (a fight) or 갈등 (conflict).
mistakes: Confusing 화해 (people making up) with 평화 (peace as in no war/calm); 화해 is interpersonal reconciliation
Saying 화해를 만들다 (make a reconciliation); just use the verb 화해하다 or 화해를 하다
